book: 206 - The Witcher and Philosophy - Toss a Coin to Your Philosopher

chapters.file: ch20 - I'm Part Elf, I'm Part Human.md
chapters.relation: Perez reads racism in Netflix's Witcher through Ibram X. Kendi's power-based account of racism, tracing the humans-versus-elves conflict through colorism (pointy ears and elven blood), 'drop rules' of racial purity that stigmatize Yennefer's quarter-elven lineage, and mutual dehumanization from Stregobor's 'mongrels' slur to Francesca's vow that the next genocide will be the humans'. He tests Kant's humanity formula against Nilfgaard's 'haven' for elves and the Battle of Aretuza, finding both sides guilty of using persons as mere means, then uses Suzy Killmister's three-strand dignity to explain why Calanthe's hidden heritage destroys her while Jaskier's Sandpiper smuggling and Cahir kneeling before Ciri restore dignity. Sartre's Other frames Yennefer's fluctuating identity between human and elf, and Dara laying down his hatred plus Ciri renouncing her power and taking the name Falka model Kendi's claim that being racist or antiracist is chosen moment by moment.

chapters.file: ch22 - Magic and the Elder Speech.md
chapters.relation: Ivanchenko argues that spells in Sapkowski's saga work as speech acts: an Elder Speech formula, correctly uttered by an authorized mage with the right gesture and drawn elemental force, changes the world simply by declaring it changed. He reads Yennefer's lessons to Ciri and Avallac'h's silent 'elven fashion' casting through Malinowski's anthropology of Trobriand magic and Durkheim on ritual formulae, then maps actual Witcher formulae ('Aine verseos!', 'Aenye!') onto Austin's performative utterances and Searle's declaratives, which 'make their propositional content true.' Failed spells - Ciri's fumbled hand gestures, her failing to draw force in the desert, Triss accidentally inventing Merigold's Destructive Hailstorm with a cut mouth - show the felicity conditions of magic in action.

Tomkinson uses Frege's sense/reference distinction (the morning star and the evening star) to ask what Sapkowski's proper names mean and pick out: Zireael ('swallow') tying Ciri to the Tower of the Swallow, Ciri's defiant adoption of 'Falka' as nom de guerre, and Regis's mule named 'Dracul' pointing both to the beast and to Count Dracula. She traces the Elder Speech's Celtic sound to Tolkien's glossopoeia and Le Guin's Earthsea true names, and reads place names like Cintra (the 1808 Convention of Cintra) as political allusions to partitioned Poland caught between empires. The chapter closes on whether fictional names like 'the Witcher' - the novels, Henry Cavill, Liam Hemsworth - have referents at all, invoking Russell's 'non-entities' and speculating that Ciri's portals and the Conjunction make the alluded worlds part of the Witcherverse itself.

chapters.file: ch24 - Between Two Camps in the Witcher.md
chapters.relation: Kammerer reads the Witcherverse's magic through the fault line between 'big tent' Platonism (top-down causation from a source, a great chain of being of nested celestial spheres) and modern naturalism (bottom-up mechanism). The Season of Storms exchange in which Geralt tells Dandelion that meteoric swords gather power descending through elemental planes - without denying those planes exist - shows Sapkowski keeping both worldviews alive, while Novigrad's Eternal Fire pogrom in The Witcher 3 mirrors fourth-century Alexandria's wars over magic and Christianity. Heidegger's 'metaphysics grounds an age' and his critique of enframing nature as standing-reserve frame Yennefer's instrumental view of magic and her djinn-summoning in The Last Wish, and Plotinus's Enneads supplies the vision of true magic as internal to a cosmic emanation rather than a mere technology.

chapters.file: ch25 - Witch Hunts Will Never Be Over.md
chapters.relation: Smock applies Girard's mimetic theory to the Witcherverse: at Calanthe's betrothal ball for Pavetta, suitors' imitated desire escalates into an all-against-all brawl in which Duny and Geralt, a monster and a mutant bearing the marks of victims, would have been scapegoated had Pavetta's magic not interrupted. He then runs Girard's four stereotypes of persecution through The Witcher 3's Novigrad, where war refugees and gang wars dissolve social differences, the Church of the Eternal Fire blames mages and nonhumans (Moritz burned at the stake, Triss's fingernails torn out by Menge), and the mob's cathartic violence resolves nothing since Emhyr's and Radovid's armies remain outside the walls. Geralt's refusal to kill Duny and his treating the rival as a person model Girard's way out of the scapegoating cycle.

chapters.file: ch27 - The Witcher as Postmodern Fairy Tale.md
chapters.relation: Vega and Barta argue The Witcher is a 'postmodern fairytale' in Lyotard's sense of incredulity toward metanarratives: the saga uses the forms of fairytales while doubting them. Jaskier's ballads (and Geralt's 'a story is a largely false account, of largely trivial events, fed to us by historians who are largely idiots') expose how lore constructs and misrepresents its subjects; 'The Lesser Evil,' the cursed-moon skepticism about Stregobor's story, and the 'grain of truth' in 'true love breaks a spell' make Geralt and the reader distrust destiny and fable morals - Ciri demands a moral from Geralt's fable and gets only 'Survive.' Adaptation across books, the Netflix show, and choice-driven games (Triss versus Yennefer, the branching Ciri endings, the ambiguous close of The Lady of the Lake) demolishes any single canonical, authoritative telling of the story.

Shores reads witchers and the Law of Surprise through Deleuze's figure of the sorcerer, the anomaly at the edge of the village who mutates through 'nuptials against nature' with unforeseeable outcomes - like the Trial of Grasses, which kills most initiates and leaves survivors infertile outcasts. He shows that the Law of Surprise, in Calanthe's words 'a game with chance, a game with destiny,' is exactly Deleuze's Nietzschean dicethrow: the throw affirms chance, the falling dice affirm necessity, an amor fati completed only through co-fated mutual affirmation ('the Sword of Destiny has two blades') among Geralt, Pavetta, and Ciri, with Chrysippus's co-fatedness supplying the logic. Pavetta's devastating cry at the betrothal banquet, scattering furniture and throne, figures the 'diabolical powers of the future' erupting into a contested present.

Crippen reads the Continent's Great Frost and the Conjunction of the Spheres as apocalypse in the word's literal sense of 'uncovering,' binding environmental collapse, refugee migration, and a post-truth erosion of moral concepts into one crisis. Nietzsche's 'inverse cripples' and Plato's Phaedo (philosophy as preparation for death, truth as lifeless unchanging perfection) illuminate Yennefer's ageless barrenness and the witchers' suppressed emotions, while Degerlund's transhumanist breeding schemes and plans to cut out Geralt's eyes violate Kantian respect for persons. Filavandrel's starving elves parallel Indigenous dispossession, Dorregaray's 'natural equilibrium' and Zoltan's prediction that humans 'wait for a chance to make money from other people's mishaps' evoke ecological and social imbalance, and Geralt's old-fashioned virtues answer a post-apocalyptic, post-truth world.

chapters.file: ch31 - King Foltest, John Locke, and the Social Contract.md
chapters.relation: Irish tests King Foltest's rule over Temeria against Locke's Two Treatises of Government: against Filmer's patriarchal divine right and Bodin's absolute sovereignty, Locke's political voluntarism holds that legitimate rule rests on the consent of free and equal subjects and exists to protect their lives, liberties, and property. Foltest's inherited throne lacks any social contract, and his edict protecting the striga Adda - the daughter born of his incest with his sister, who preys on Wyzim's citizens - breaches the Lockean sovereign trust. The Netflix 'Betrayer Moon' miners' uprising becomes a Lockean revolution: after 'a long train of abuses' the people may reclaim the sovereign power and even remove the king, so long as the new authority restores consent and the public good.

Van der Zee uses Schmitt's concept of 'the political' - the friend/enemy distinction whose utmost intensity is the possibility of war - to explain why Geralt's witcher neutrality keeps failing, from the choice over the Scoia'tael taking Haren Brogg's goods in the game's Outskirts to the Salamandra theft of the mutagens from Kaer Morhen. Schmitt's claim that a group unwilling to defend its way of existence must surrender its fate to those who will fight explains why the witchers' pursuit of the stolen mutagens drags Geralt into Temerian politics and the Order of the Flaming Rose's schemes. The chapter's sharpest point is that 'monster' names the dangerous complement of Schmitt's 'humanity': witcher neutrality is only sustainable in a world where enemies remain respected enemies, not monsters to be exterminated, which is why Geralt refuses Commander Wenck's request to hunt Scoia'tael as 'evil creatures.'

chapters.file: ch33 - Sometimes You Have to Fight.md
chapters.relation: Brake pits Geralt's refusal to choose between evils ('Evil is evil, Stregobor... if I'm to choose between one evil and another, then I prefer not to choose at all') against Reinhold Niebuhr's Christian realism, which holds that collective political life admits only greater and lesser evils and 'enough justice,' never the individual's moral purity. Triss's post-Sodden realization that war is survival rather than a choice, Ciri's verdict that Geralt's neutrality was contemptible, and Nilfgaard's 'war on everything that can burn' push toward Niebuhr's view that capitulation to tyranny in the name of nonresistant perfection becomes connivance. Yet Yarpen's herd-of-pigs defense of progress and the fate of the Nilfgaardian settlers driven out of Rivia after victory show that even relative justice stays stained, which is why witchers, as Yarpen says, 'will always be needed.'

chapters.file: ch34 - Origin and Desires as Monster Makers in the Witcher.md
chapters.relation: Swanstrom and Lyle test medieval theories of monstrosity against the show: Stregobor's Curse of the Black Sun echoes Aristotle's, Avicenna's, and Aquinas's celestial-influence explanations of fetal mutation (though even they would not convict Renfri by birthday alone), while Yennefer's spine and infertility invoke Aquinas on failed generation and women as 'deformed males,' with witchers cast as Aquinas's mules - an engineered, infertile natural kind. They argue that neither origin nor appearance but motivation and virtue make a monster: Renfri's revenge, Nivellen's rape of the priestess, and Stregobor's vivisection of girls are Aristotelian 'bestial' habit and vicious character, not mean-relative virtue. Geralt's shifting telos, from monster-slayer protecting humans to protector of Ciri (knighted by Queen Meve), shows even a mutant can develop virtue, so mutations, heritage, and gender cannot be what monstrosity is.

chapters.file: ch35 - The Witcher and the Monstrous Feminine.md
chapters.relation: Cameron reads Geralt's battles with the striga (Foltest's cursed daughter by his sister Adda) and the bruxa Vereena in 'A Grain of Truth' through French feminist theory: Cixous's claim that women are frozen 'between the Medusa and the abyss,' Irigaray's reading of Nietzsche's feminine hysteria, and Kristeva's abject maternal in Powers of Horror. Both stories are phallocentric - men deliberate while Adda never speaks and Vereena can only scream - and in both the female monster is sacrificed to restore the symbolic order, Nivellen's curse broken by Vereena's death at Geralt's silver sword. Geralt himself is abjected: bitten and bled by the striga in her own crypt, nursed wounded at the Temple of Melitele, he becomes permeable and monstrous in her place, paying the cost of policing the patriarchal boundary.

Giladi argues the Witcherverse's silver/steel sword dualism - the clean division between 'human' and 'monster' - is subverted by what he calls the dialectics of monstrosity: the worst monsters are moral ones, agents cruel through and through. He reads the 'Killing Monsters' trailer (Geralt hanging the Nilfgaardian officer about to hang a young woman), the witch hunter exchange ('you don't need mutations to strip men of their humanity'), Tissaia's torture of Cahir, and Stregobor's autopsy plans through Honneth's Hegelian account of recognition (losing 'antecedent recognition') and Shklar's cruelty as the summum malum. Montaigne on recreational cruelty and Arendt's banality of evil explain Geralt's genealogy that 'people like to invent monsters... then they seem less monstrous themselves,' while Bernard Williams shows Geralt's 'Evil is Evil' refusal to get his hands dirty is itself what lets evil fester.

holes.name: Ibram X. Kendi
holes.what: Contemporary historian and antiracism theorist who defines racism as rooted in racist policy and power, and holds that one is in each moment either being racist or being antiracist.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire framework - colorism, the 'drop rules,' dehumanization, and Ciri's antiracist choice - is built on Kendi's How to Be an Antiracist, and no existing taxonomy slug covers him.

holes.name: Bronislaw Malinowski
holes.what: Anthropologist whose studies of Trobriand magic analyzed the spell as traditional words whose utterance generates and conveys a magical force (mana) toward an aim.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is organized around Malinowski's theory of verbal magic as the key to how Elder Speech spell-casting works, alongside Austin and Searle.

holes.name: Speech Acts (performative utterances)
holes.what: The theory that some utterances (performatives and declaratives) do not describe the world but perform an act, changing the world by saying so under felicity conditions.
holes.why: Chapter 22's central claim is that Witcher spells are performative speech acts - Austin's performatives and Searle's declaratives - and the taxonomy has no concept slug for speech act theory.

holes.name: Mimetic Desire
holes.what: Girard's thesis that desire is not spontaneous but copied from a model or mediator, so rivals imitating the same object escalate into mimetic rivalry and crisis.
holes.why: Chapter 25 explains the Pavetta betrothal brawl and the Novigrad witch hunts through mimetic desire and mimetic crisis, concepts the taxonomy lacks despite having Girard.

holes.name: The Scapegoat Mechanism
holes.what: Girard's account of how a crisis of all-against-all violence is resolved by unanimous violence against a marked victim, whose persecution reunites the community without solving its causes.
holes.why: Chapter 25's core argument is that the Eternal Fire's persecution of mages, elves, and witchers is Girardian scapegoating with the four stereotypes of persecution.

holes.name: Becoming-Other (the Deleuzian sorcerer)
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's notion of mutation without preset outcome: the sorcerer as anomaly at the fringes who enters 'nuptials against nature' and cannot know in advance what they will become.
holes.why: Chapter 28 maps witchers, the Trial of Grasses, and the Law of Surprise onto Deleuze's sorcerer and becoming-other, a notion the taxonomy's 'rhizome' does not capture.

holes.name: Reinhold Niebuhr
holes.what: Twentieth-century political theologian whose Christian realism (Moral Man and Immoral Society) holds that collective life can achieve only relative justice and lesser evils, never individual moral purity.
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues against Geralt's 'Evil is evil' neutrality entirely through Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society; the taxonomy has only H. Richard Niebuhr, a different thinker.

holes.name: Helene Cixous
holes.what: French feminist theorist of ecriture feminine who, in 'Sorties' and The Newly Born Woman, analyzes how women are frozen between the Medusa and the abyss in the patriarchal symbolic order.
holes.why: Chapter 35 draws equally on Cixous (with Kristeva) to read the striga and the bruxa as the monstrous feminine, and Cixous is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Axel Honneth
holes.what: Third-generation Frankfurt School theorist whose theory of recognition (self-confidence, self-respect, self-esteem, and antecedent recognition) derives from Hegel's forms of intersubjectivity.
holes.why: Chapter 36 explains moral monstrosity as losing antecedent recognition using Honneth's Struggle for Recognition and Reification as its main framework after Hegel himself.
